sources.news_title: Canada reimposes sanctions on 11 Iranian entities
sources.text:
Canada has reimposed sanctions on 11 Iranian entities, including major banks, oil companies and nuclear-related firms, reversing sanctions relief granted in 2016 under the Iran nuclear deal, according to Global Affairs Canada.
The sanctioned entities include the National Iranian Oil Company, National Iranian Tanker Company, Bank Melli Iran and Bank Mellat. The measures prohibit specified financial and property transactions involving Canadians and are intended to restrict Iran's access to funding and sensitive technologies.
Canada lifted the restrictions in 2016 following Iran's initial compliance with the nuclear agreement. The decision to restore them follows renewed concerns over Iran's nuclear activities and the reinstatement of U.N. sanctions in September 2025 after Tehran failed to meet its nuclear obligations.

Canada reimposes sanctions on 11 Iranian entities over nuclear proliferation, missile programme
sources.text:
Canada reimposes sanctions on 11 Iranian entities over nuclear proliferation, missile programme
Canada foreign minister Anita Anand announced the measures at a meeting of Group of Seven foreign ministers in Paris.
Canada reimposed sanctions on 11 Iranian entities on Tuesday for their contribution to Iran's nuclear activities and ballistic missile program, Foreign Minister Anita Anand said.
Anand announced the measures at a meeting of Group of Seven foreign ministers in Paris, saying they were intended to restrict Iran's access to funding and sensitive technology linked to its nuclear and missile programs.
"Canada’s position is unequivocal: Iran must never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon," a foreign ministry statement quoted Anand as saying.
The measures were imposed on 11 entities that contributed to "the Iranian regime’s proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities and ballistic missile program or to the financing of its malign activities," the statement said.
ALSO READ: Trump says US war in Iran is ‘militarily effectively over', suggests ‘status quo’ to continue
Canada de-listed the entities in 2016 after a 2015 nuclear deal between Iran and world powers. But Ottawa said Tehran had repeatedly failed to cooperate with the International Atomic Energy Agency, the UN nuclear watchdog, over its nuclear activities and had not complied with the provisions of earlier UN Security Council resolutions.
The United States, its European allies and Israel accuse Tehran of using its nuclear program to conceal efforts to try to develop the capability to produce weapons. Iran says its nuclear program is for peaceful purposes only.
The US has been at war with Iran since joint US-Israeli airstrikes against the Islamic Republic on February 28.
ALSO READ: Marco Rubio says peace talks with Iran 'not very productive,' calls Tehran's demands ‘outrageous’
An Iranian official told Reuters last week that Tehran had submitted a proposal on nuclear issues to the US via Qatar, but that discussions would depend on Washington first meeting a set of Iranian demands.
The demands include sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and war reparations, the official said. Washington says nuclear issues must feature in initial talks.
The 11 entities targeted by Canada include Iran's Nuclear Fuel Production and Procurement Company, the Nuclear Reactors Fuel Company, the National Iranian Oil Company and the National Iranian Tanker Company.
The other sanctioned entities include Kala Naft, the Naftiran Intertrade Company, Bank Mellat, Bank Melli, the Iran Bank of Industry and Mine, the Export Development Bank of Iran and the Iran Insurance Company.
Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, said in October that Tehran was debating whether to lift its longstanding ban on nuclear weapons if hostilities resume, although he said no such decision had been taken yet.

Canada Reimposes Sanctions Against 11 Iranian Companies
sources.text:
Canada on Tuesday said it was reimposing sanctions against 11 Iranian companies in the energy and banking sectors for contributing to the Islamic republic’s nuclear drive, ballistic missile programme or the financing of “malign activities”.
The companies, which include the National Iranian Oil Company and leading banks Mellat and Melli, were delisted from Canadian sanctions in 2016. But the measures have now been reimposed “to disrupt Iranian financial networks supporting its nuclear program”, the Canadian foreign ministry said in a statement on the sidelines of the G7 meeting in Paris.
AFP

sources.news_title: Canada reimposes sanctions on 11 entities over Iranian non-compliance with nuclear obligations
sources.text:
Canada reimposed sanctions against 11 Iranian entities on Tuesday over concerns regarding Iran’s nuclear program and Tehran’s refusal to cooperate with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Foreign Minister Anita Anand confirmed.
Sanctions against the entities, which include Iranian nuclear procurement companies, oil companies, and banks, were previously lifted in 2016 “in recognition of Iran’s progress under the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA),” according to Canada’s foreign ministry.
Canada, Iran, the US, the EU, and other countries agreed to the JCPOA in 2015 after Iran failed to meet obligations related to its nuclear commitments.
Under the JCPOA, Tehran agreed to be subject to restrictions on its nuclear program and enhanced IAEA verification in exchange for the relaxation of sanctions.
Iran found to be violating JCPOA terms, not cooperating with IAEA
Despite initially complying with the terms of the JCPOA, in June 2025, the IAEA found that Iran was not fully complying with the terms.
When the US and Israel launched strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities in July 2025, Iran suspended cooperation with the IAEA and prevented the nuclear watchdog from fulfilling verification and monitoring duties.
The non-compliance and continued production of enriched uranium triggered the reinstatement of UN sanctions, eventually leading to Canada also reinstating some sanctions.

sources.news_title: Canada puts Iranian tanker giant back under sanctions
sources.text:
Canada puts Iranian tanker giant back under sanctions
Canada has reinstated sanctions against the National Iranian Tanker Company (NITC), reversing relief granted a decade ago under the international nuclear agreement with Tehran.
The move forms part of a package targeting 11 Iranian entities, including National Iranian Oil Company (NIOC), oil trading group Naftiran Intertrade and several major financial institutions.
The measures were announced by Canadian foreign minister Anita Anand during a G7 foreign ministers’ meeting in Paris.
The restrictions prohibit specified dealings involving the property of sanctioned entities and related financial services by people and businesses in Canada, as well as Canadians operating abroad.
The decision puts NITC back under Canadian restrictions for the first time since February 2016, when Ottawa removed the company and several other Iranian organisations from its sanctions list following implementation of the nuclear agreement.
NITC is one of the world’s major crude tanker operators and a central player in Iran’s seaborne oil exports. The company already faces extensive US restrictions, with tankers associated with its operations repeatedly targeted under measures aimed at limiting Iran’s oil revenues.
Canada said the latest action follows renewed concerns over Iran’s nuclear programme and cooperation with international inspectors. The decision comes after United Nations nuclear-related sanctions were reinstated in September 2025.
The government said the renewed listings are intended to further restrict Iranian access to financial resources and sensitive technologies.

sources.news_title: Canada reimposes sanctions against 11 Iranian companies - Newsy People
sources.text:
News
                            
Canada’s foreign ministry announced the measures on the sidelines of the G7 meeting in Paris, saying they were intended “to disrupt Iranian financial networks supporting its nuclear program”. All 11 entities were removed from Canada’s sanctions list in 2016 after international inspectors reported that Iran had taken steps to meet its commitments under the 2015 nuclear deal.
The entities are the Nuclear Fuel Production and Procurement Company, Nuclear Reactors Fuel Company, Kala Naft, Naftiran Intertrade Company, National Iranian Oil Company, National Iranian Tanker Company, Bank Mellat, Bank Melli Iran, Bank of Industry and Mine, Export Development Bank of Iran and Iran Insurance Company.
The measures were reinstated under Canada’s Special Economic Measures (Iran) Regulations. Ottawa said they would further restrict Iran’s access to sensitive technology and funding. The regulations prohibit people in Canada and Canadians abroad from carrying out specified financial or property transactions with listed individuals and entities.
Canada first imposed sanctions under those regulations in July 2010, in consultation with partners including the United States and the European Union, citing Iran’s failure to meet its international nuclear obligations. As a non-nuclear-weapon state under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, Iran is obliged not to develop or acquire nuclear weapons.
In July 2015, China, France, Germany, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States, together with the European Union, reached an agreement with Iran known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA). Endorsed by UN Security Council Resolution 2231, the deal imposed limits on Iran’s nuclear programme and expanded verification by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), including through the Additional Protocol, in exchange for sanctions relief.
The IAEA reported in January 2016 that Iran had allowed verification activities and taken steps to restrict its nuclear programme under the agreement. Canada eased its own sanctions the following month in coordination with international partners, removing the 11 entities from its list.
In June 2025, the IAEA Board of Governors found that Iran was not complying with its safeguards obligations and called on Tehran to cooperate fully with inspectors. The following month, after Israeli and US attacks on Iran, Tehran suspended cooperation with the agency, further limiting its ability to monitor and verify nuclear activities.
France, Germany and the UK invoked the agreement’s “snapback” mechanism in August 2025, citing Iran’s production of highly enriched uranium and insufficient cooperation with the IAEA. The move led to the reinstatement of UN nuclear-related sanctions in September. Canada amended its separate regulations implementing UN resolutions on Iran that month to give effect to those measures.
In June 2026, the G7 reaffirmed that Iran must not develop or acquire a nuclear weapon and called for limits on uranium enrichment and effective IAEA verification.

sources.news_title: Carney backs more war on Iran & Yemen
sources.text:
Carney backs more war on Iran and killing Yemeni civilians.
Today Global Affairs announced sanctions on 11 major Iranian banks and companies. Ottawa is prohibiting people in Canada and Canadians abroad from transacting with the National Iranian Oil Company, Export Development Bank of Iran, Iran Insurance Company and other institutions.
According to the government, Canada de-listed the entities in 2016 after Iran signed the JCPOA nuclear deal, which Donald Trump subsequently ripped up. Now foreign minister Anita Anand said Canada was reimposing sanctions against them “for contributing to the Iranian regime’s proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities and ballistic missile program or to the financing of its malign activities.”
But, Iran doesn’t have nuclear arms and is a member of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT). Conversely, Israel has nukes and is the only country in the region not part of the NPT, yet Ottawa hasn’t sanctioned Israeli entities contributing to its nuclear arms program. Israel also has a ballistic missile program capable of hitting cities as far away as eastern Canada. That country has also engaged in an endless stream of “malign activities” across the region and world.
Canada’s latest round of sanctions come amidst US/Israeli preparations to restart significant bombing of Iran. They also come soon after the US public rejected Trump’s war in the mid-term elections (from the get-go the US public was ambivalent about the aggression, but Iran’s ability to impact people in the US, notably through higher gas prices, galvanized opposition).
US vice president JD Vance cited the war and ties to Israel as central factors in the Republicans’ disastrous election results. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham also said the outcome of the US midterms offered an “opportunity” to resolve the conflict with Iran.
Instead of bolstering those seeking to deescalate the war, the Mark Carney government is imposing a new round of harsh sanctions on Iran!
At the same time, Carney is encouraging a Saudi Arabian monarchy fighting an ally of Iran. On Monday, the Prime Minister spoke with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, “condemning Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia” and affirming “Canada’s solidarity with the Kingdom”, according to Saudi media. But, the Saudis have killed nearly 100 Yemeni civilians already this month. On Saturday the Saudis killed several dozen in Yemen’s Sanaa Province. Antiwar.com reported:
“The death toll in Saudi airstrikes that hit civilian homes in the Bani Hashish District of Yemen’s Sanaa province on Saturday has risen to 44, according to the Health Ministry within the Sanaa-based Ansar Allah-led Yemeni government.
“The death toll makes the attack the worst civilian massacre committed by the US-backed Saudi coalition since Riyadh reignited the war back in July by bombing the Sanaa International Airport.
“According to Health Ministry spokesman Dr. Anis al-Asbahi, who announced the updated death toll, 21 children and 10 women were among those killed. Another 40 Yemenis, including eight children and nine women, were wounded.
“The strike came a day after Ansar Allah, the Houthis, said that Saudi airstrikes hit a crowded market in the southwestern Taiz province, killing at least 30 people. The Saudi-backed Yemeni government claimed the market was hit by Houthi ballistic missiles, but it provided no evidence for the claim, and the Saudi bombing campaign has been killing scores of civilians.
“According to the Yemen Data Project, the Saudi bombing campaign killed at least 140 civilians and wounded 286 in October, making it the worst month for civilian harm from Saudi airstrikes in Yemen since December 2017.”
Carney hasn’t said a peep about the hundreds of Yemeni civilians killed by Saudi airstrikes. But, his government has repeatedly condemned Ansar Allah’s much less murderous strikes on Saudi Arabia.
Mark Carney’s endless hypocrisy must be repeatedly denounced. Canada is enabling significant violence.

sources.news_title: Canada reimposes sanctions on 11 Iranian entities, targeting key sectors
sources.text:
Canada’s Foreign Minister Anita Anand has announced the reimposition of sanctions on 11 Iranian entities. This move forms part of Canada’s broader strategy to exert pressure on Iran, targeting its security, intelligence, censorship, and economic sectors. The sanctions are designed to restrict dealings with these entities and freeze their assets in Canada. This development marks the continuation of Canada’s robust sanctions regime against Iran, which has been expanding since October 2022.
Key Takeaways
- The announcement appears to reinforce Canada’s firm stance against Iran’s current policies, maintaining economic and legal pressure.
- Markets suggest this move could increase the likelihood of political instability within Iran, potentially affecting leadership dynamics.
- The reimposition of sanctions is consistent with scenarios where international discontent with Iran’s actions is escalating.
What to Watch
Observers will be monitoring any shifts in political dynamics within Iran, particularly regarding President Masoud Pezeshkian’s competitive position. The impact of these sanctions on Iran’s internal politics and international relations will be crucial. Watch for any statements from Iranian leadership or retaliatory measures that could further strain Iran’s foreign relations. These developments may influence the perception of Pezeshkian’s leadership stability in the coming weeks.
